lessonPlan.title: Frankenstein unit
lessonPlan.author: Mary Shelley
lessonPlan.editionNote: The reading text is Mary Shelley's revised 1831 edition (Standard Ebooks, from Project Gutenberg #42324), which also prints the 1818 Preface and the 1831 Introduction. In 1818 Elizabeth is Victor's cousin; in 1831 she is the orphaned daughter of a Milanese nobleman, adopted by Victor's mother. Chapter breaks also differ (e.g. around Chapter III). Cite this edition.
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 9–12 (also 7–8; scales to graduate via rigor levels)
lessonPlan.middleSchoolTrack: Excerpt-based support track: these novels are above the grades 6–8 text-complexity band, so Middle School prompts work from teacher-selected passages.
lessonPlan.schedule: 30 chapter lessons plus 3 seminar day(s), a test day and an essay day: 35 class days of 90 minutes, 5 a week (block schedule), 7 weeks
essentialQuestions: What does Frankenstein suggest about the costs of unchecked ambition?
What does Frankenstein suggest about creation and responsibility?
What does Frankenstein suggest about isolation and the need for companionship?
What does Frankenstein suggest about nature versus nurture?
What does Frankenstein suggest about the sublime power of nature?
objectives: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly and implicitly.
Determine themes and analyze their development over the course of the novel.
Analyze how characters, setting and point of view interact.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.

lessonPlan.contentNote: The novel includes suicide, the murder of a child, a wrongful execution and the murder of a bride; see the chapter notes and the safe-messaging script.
assessments: Final essay (scheduled day); College Sophomore and above write one essay of the five
lessonPlan.differentiation: Every prompt and quiz has eleven rigor levels (Middle School through Graduate / PhD); the app applies student override, then class standard, then the automatic level. Each prompt is tagged for Common Core, Indiana 2023, Dual Credit (Indiana College Core), AP and Cambridge where they apply.

wholeBookTest.title: Frankenstein: whole-book test

items.prompt: Where was Shelley staying when the ghost-story contest began?
options: On a ship to the Arctic

items.prompt: Which scientist does the Preface mention as having supposed the event possible?
To whom is Walton writing?
What does Walton say he lacks most?
options: A friend who shares his feelings

items.prompt: How does Walton feel in Letter III?
What does the crew first see on the ice?
options: A gigantic figure on a dog sled

items.prompt: Where is Victor's family from?
Which author first fascinates Victor?
How does Victor's mother die?
What does Victor discover?
options: The cause of generation and life

items.prompt: What month does the creature come to life?
Who writes to Victor during his recovery?
Who has been murdered?
What happens at Justine's trial?
What does Victor's despair lead him to contemplate?
Where does Victor meet the creature?
Who narrates this chapter?
Whom does the creature observe?
Who arrives at the cottage?
Why were the De Laceys exiled?
options: Felix helped a Turkish merchant escape

items.prompt: Which book is NOT among those he finds?
Where does the creature travel after the De Laceys leave?
What does the creature demand?
Why does Victor travel to England?
options: To create the female in secret

items.prompt: Where does Victor work on the second creature?
options: A remote island in the Orkneys

items.prompt: Why does Victor destroy the female?
options: He fears a race of devils

items.prompt: Who is the murdered man?
Who travels with Victor to Paris and cares for him there?
Where does Elizabeth's murder take place?
What do Walton's crew demand?

answerKey.answer: A friend who shares his feelings
A gigantic figure on a dog sled
The cause of generation and life
Felix helped a Turkish merchant escape
To create the female in secret
A remote island in the Orkneys
He fears a race of devils

shortAnswer: Explain how the costs of unchecked ambition develops from the beginning of the novel to the end. Use two chapters.
Explain how creation and responsibility develops from the beginning of the novel to the end. Use two chapters.
Explain how isolation and the need for companionship develops from the beginning of the novel to the end. Use two chapters.
wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the novel's central concerns (the costs of unchecked ambition, creation and responsibility, isolation and the need for companionship, nature versus nurture, the sublime power of nature) and argue how the ending reframes it.

essayAssignments.title: Essay: The costs of unchecked ambition

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what Frankenstein teaches about the costs of unchecked ambition. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Mary Shelley develops the costs of unchecked ambition in Frankenstein. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Mary Shelley develops the costs of unchecked ambition across Frankenstein. Trace the idea through at least three chapters and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of Frankenstein (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of the costs of unchecked ambition. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of the costs of unchecked ambition in Frankenstein. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Mary Shelley's choices in Frankenstein (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of the costs of unchecked ambition, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places Frankenstein's treatment of the costs of unchecked ambition in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on the costs of unchecked ambition in Frankenstein that reads the novel against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on the costs of unchecked ambition in Frankenstein. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about the costs of unchecked ambition in Frankenstein, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on the costs of unchecked ambition in Frankenstein, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
